title: Arrival clustering and backpressure scratchpad
body:
Goal: explore how clustered arrivals (short bursts of tightly-packed requests) interact with the batcher/backpressure path and KV cache behavior. Want concrete knobs to reduce 99th pct tail without sacrificing throughput.

Hypothesis: clusters cause transient queueing in the batcher which (a) increases scheduling latency for later requests in-cluster and (b) misaligns KV cache warmup, causing higher per-token work. Introducing conservative backpressure (soft drop or increased batching timeout for cluster windows) and adaptive prefetching of KV cache should reduce p99 with modest throughput impact.

Experiment summary (single-run notes):
- model: open-llm/7B-quant (local test image built from serving-runtime:bench-2025-10)
- infra: 1 x a100-40GB (dedicated dev node), driver node for loadgen on c5a.4x; containerized runtime with default batcher.
- load generator: custom harness (arrival-cluster mode) built on top of vegeta; emits clusters of N requests over cluster_window_ms then idles for gap_ms.
- test config used today: cluster_size=40, cluster_window_ms=1200, gap_ms=9000, request_qps_peak≈33 inside cluster, payload token length 64 avg, KV cache enabled.
- duration: 30m (warmup 5m, measurement 20m, cooldown 5m)

Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end), server scheduling latency (time in batch queue), batch sizes distribution, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, request drop/backpressure events, end-to-end throughput (req/s), tail queue length samples.

Raw observations (picked highlights):
- steady-state throughput =~ 85 req/s outside clusters, inside clusters instantaneous throughput went to 120 req/s while batcher queue length spiked to 600ms average wait.
- p50: 36ms, p95: 210ms, p99: 570ms (within cluster). Outside clusters p99 settled to ~140ms.
- scheduling latency accounted for ~65% of p99 spikes during clusters. Batch sizes grew (median 8 -> 18) but variance increased a lot leading to head-of-line blocking.
- KV cache hit rate dropped by ~12 percentage points shortly after clusters (suggests new prefixes cause cache churn).
- GPU util stayed high (~86%) so not pure compute saturation; the big contributor was queueing & scheduling alignment.
- We observed 2 soft-backpressure events (runtime signaled overload) when peak cluster QPS briefly exceeded allowed inflight windows. Those events correlated with small number of client retries in the harness (we intentionally retried once).

Quick visual notes (charts stored in run folder):
- run-2025-11-18/charts/arrival-clusters-queue-length.png -> shows periodic spikes aligned with cluster windows.
- run-2025-11-18/charts/p99-by-window.png -> p99 jumps inside windows, step-decay afterward.
- run-2025-11-18/logs/trace-sample-1123.json -> sampling of scheduling events.

Initial conclusions / takeaways:
1) Clustering increases p99 primarily via scheduling/queue wait, not raw GPU execution time. Means we should tune batcher/backpressure rather than change model.
2) Larger batches in clusters help amortize compute, but increased variance causes head-of-line blocking for low-latency requests inside the same cluster.
3) KV cache effects: cluster arrivals with varied prefixes cause cache churn; small prefetch or pinning hot prefixes per-tenant might help.
4) Soft-backpressure is useful but needs better client-facing signaling (Retry-After or adaptive token bucket) to avoid tight client retries that amplify clusters.

Immediate experiments to run next (prioritized):
- A: batcher timeout sweep (50, 100, 250, 500 ms) with cluster_size fixed at 40 to find sweet-spot that reduces p99 inside clusters while keeping throughput.
- B: enable "cluster-aware" micro-backpressure: if queueing > X ms, temporarily increase per-tenant batching timeout to allow larger batches to form, then revert. Test X in {200, 400, 600}.
- C: KV cache pinning: for synthetic workloads, pin top-10 prefixes and re-run to quantify hit-rate impact on latency during clusters.
- D: client backoff strategy: change harness to use exponential backoff on retry (base 25ms) to see if retries reduce tail amplification.

Action items (who/when):
- Samir: add batcher timeout param to bench image and run A/B sweep, target 2025-11-21.
- Maya: instrument KV cache eviction trace to confirm churn causes and export a time-correlated graph, target 2025-11-22.
- Evan: prototype client retry policy in harness and run comparative test, target 2025-11-24.
- Me (Talia): collect end-to-end traces and prepare short doc with recommended default batcher/backpressure settings for internal runbook, draft by 2025-11-28.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Is head-of-line blocking worsened when multiple tenants with different SLOs share the same worker? Need a multi-tenant run.
- Could adaptive timeout increase tail latency for single-request clients outside clusters? Watch for regressions.
- Consider a fast-path: small-sla class bypassing the coalescing window to avoid waiting for large batches. Complexity tradeoffs need evaluation.

Links / references:
- Related ticket: JIRA-4821 ("Investigate cluster-induced p99 spikes")
- PR with initial backpressure signal proposal: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842
- Slack thread: #bench-results (https://slack.com/archives/C02XYZ/p1678901234567890)

Notes to future me: include multi-tenant run asap; simulate mixed-size payloads (16, 64, 256 tokens) to test cache sensitivity. If we get consistent p99 reductions with conservative adaptive backpressure, roll into canary for dedicated nodes behind a feature flag.

End of scratchpad.
